item.title: What is Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor trying to say?
item.description: It is less about moral values but the product of a desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.
item.content:encoded:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticised him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie A Bug’s Life in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

item.title: Bar Council halts NALSAR student enrolment over campaign against CJI, withdraws order hours later
item.description: Political campaign Cockroach Janta Party had warned of protests by law students and advocates if the council did not take back the directive.
item.content:encoded:
The Bar Council of India on Thursday withdrew an order directing state bar councils to defer the enrolment of any student of the National Academy of Legal Studies and Research graduating in 2026 who opposed the participation of Chief Justice Surya Kant at the university’s convocation.

However, the council has said that an inquiry into those who were “principally instrumental” in a campaign against the chief justice’s participation would continue.

Political campaign Cockroach Janta Party had described the directive as “grossly disproportionate” and had warned of protests by law students and advocates if it was not taken back.

Abhijeet Dipke, founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, asked, “What if all legal cockroaches come together?”

Condemning the order, CJP Spokesperson Saurav Das said that students cannot be “collectively penalised for expressing dissent over a ceremonial invitation”.

Das had warned of a protest outside Bar Council’s office and Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra’s official residence by law students, advocates, senior lawyers, and “well-meaning young cockroaches”, if the order was not withdrawn.

item.title: Remove pre-ride tipping prompts from apps, transport ministry tells vehicle aggregators
item.description: The ministry pointed to the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, which state that passengers have the option of tipping drivers only after the trip is complete.
item.content:encoded:
The Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has asked ride-hailing platforms to remove prompts from their mobile applications that encourage customers to tip the driver at the time of booking, the Deccan Herald reported on Thursday.

The ministry said that such prompts violate the 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, which state that passengers have the option to give drivers a tip only after the trip is completed.

Several vehicle aggregator platforms prompt users to tip drivers before booking a ride. These prompts include options such as “Advance Tip” and “Choose an Add-on”, with some suggesting that tipping could help secure a ride faster or increase the chances of a driver accepting the booking.

item.title: Sugarcane powers India’s rural economy but climate change is affecting yield
item.description: The crop sustains millions of farmers but concerns are growing over its water demands as the changing weather poses challenges.
item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane cultivation across parts of India’s Deccan Plateau is becoming more productive. But, it is also becoming more vulnerable to climate variability, a new long-term study finds.

Sugarcane has long shaped India’s rural economy. It powers sugar mills, supports ethanol and bioenergy production, and sustains millions of farmers. But the crop is also at the centre of mounting concerns over water use, particularly in semi-arid regions facing recurrent droughts and groundwater stress.

The study analysed 22 years of sugarcane production trends across five districts in Maharashtra and Karnataka to understand how cultivation, yields and production patterns have changed under varying climatic conditions.

“We noticed that sugarcane cultivation in Maharashtra and Karnataka was increasingly being affected by climatic variability, even though it remains one of the most important economic activities across the Deccan Plateau,” says Krishna Kumar from the Department of Applied Science and Humanities at MIT-ADT University, Pune, and one of the study’s researchers.

Across climate zones

Sugarcane production trends in India have been studied extensively at national and state levels, but long-term district-level analyses incorporating weather variability remain limited.

The march was organised as part of an agitation against alleged irregularities in competitive examinations conducted for state government jobs.

Ranchi Superintendent of Police Paras Rana told PTI that the FIR has been registered “for disrupting the peaceful march”.

The unidentified persons have also been booked for attacking police personnel during the march.

The police are trying to identify the individuals through video footage, PTI quoted Hatia Sub-Divisional Police Officer Neeraj Kumar as saying.

The protests in Jharkhand began on July 25, inspired by the agitation across the country against alleged mismanagement of national competitive examinations. The protesters have been holding a sit-in at Ranchi’s Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium.

Poor Mushtari Bano, a devout woman who was regular with her prayers and fasts and who would keep a watch on Kallo from a distance, couldn’t even in her wildest dreams imagine that the urchin would hit her nerve one day!

I first spotted Kallo at the tooth powder seller’s tamasha. Every Friday evening, a bulky man would appear with a drummer and sell assorted tooth powders. Both young and old would throng his cart.

item.description: They were facing trial for allegedly violating prohibitory orders and inciting communal tension.
item.content:encoded:
A special MP-MLA court in Uttar Pradesh on Wednesday approved the prosecution’s request to withdraw a case related to the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots against 25 Bharatiya Janata Party leaders and persons associated with Hindutva groups, PTI reported.

Communal violence had erupted in Muzaffarnagar in September 2013 after BJP leaders, including Suresh Rana, former party MLA Sangeet Som and former MP Bharatendra Singh, allegedly made inflammatory speeches.

At least 60 persons were killed and thousands of Muslim families were displaced in the riots that followed. There were also several reports of sexual assault and abuse in Muzaffarnagar and Shamli districts.

Among the accused persons facing charges in the present case were state minister Kapil Dev Agarwal, former Union Minister Sanjeev Balyan and former state minister Suresh Rana. Others include former Uttar Pradesh minister Ashok Kataria, ex-BJP MPs Bhartendu Singh and Sohanvir Singh, former BJP MLAs Ashok Kansal and Umesh Malik, Vishwa Hindu Parishad leader Sadhvi Prachi and Narsinghanand of Dasna Shiv Temple.

The Vishva Hindu Parishad is part of a group of Hindutva organisations led by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the parent organisation of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

item.title: Nisha da Cunha (1934-2026): An inspirational teacher and writer of things usually left unsaid
item.description: Her literary contribution is particularly significant for its topicality today, writes a former student.
item.content:encoded:
Some people come to us to definitively shape who we later become. Call it providence, fate, destiny, chance or sheer good luck, but Professor Nisha da Cunha, who died on August 11, was one such provocateur in my life.

My recollections of her are perhaps common to every student of English Literature at St Xavier's College of the mid- and late 1970s – the commanding air, the measured diction while reading a text aloud in the classroom, trademark poise, impatience with students who "showed off" and her passionate guidance of those she believed had potential.

It is not an exaggeration to say that we not only wanted to be as bright as she was, we actually wanted to be her, down to her short hair, piercing gaze, woven saree and large red bindi. She was simply cool. (A few years later at my first job, I mimicked an elegant "handloom" saree look. For the admiration expressed by my German bosses, the credit goes to Nisha da Cunha.)

When asked if action would be taken against Roy, the chief minister said he would not “name anyone, but the law is equal for MLAs, MPs, leaders of any party, government officials or police officers”.

Defending the Assam government’s proposal to reduce the eco-sensitive zone around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve to 1 km from 10 km, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on Wednesday the decision was in accordance with Supreme Court guidelines.

On August 8, Sarma had said the eco-sensitive zone around the UNESCO World Heritage Site, which is home to the world’s largest population of one-horned rhinoceroses, was 10 km “by default”. The Assam government would send a proposal to the Union government within two months to reduce the limit to 1 km to allow development activities in the area, including the construction of a stadium, he had added.

In June 2022, the Supreme Court ordered that eco-sensitive zones of at least 1 km should be declared around protected forests, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries.

However, in April 2023, the court modified the order after states and the Union government argued that uniformly applying the 1-km requirement was not feasible and it had to be “protected area-specific”.

item.title: HC sets aside order refusing FCRA renewal of NGOs over claims of funding protests against Adani port
item.description: The government’s ‘distaste for dissent’ cannot be grounds to say that protests were against public interest, said the Kerala High Court.
item.content:encoded:
The Kerala High Court has set aside a Union government order refusing to renew the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act registration of two non-profits on the grounds that they had funded protests against the Adani port project in Vizhinjam, reported Bar and Bench on Wednesday.

Registration under the Act is mandatory for non-profit organisations to receive foreign funds.

Even if the organisations – Kerala Social Service Forum and Save a Family Plan India – had provided financial support to protesters, it could not be treated as the use of foreign funds for an undesirable purpose, said Justice Bechu Kurian Thomas in his order on Tuesday.

In 2022, a group of fisherfolk staged protests against the Rs 7,500-crore project led by billionaire Gautam Adani’s ports business. They alleged that the project would cause coastal erosion and damage their livelihoods.

The protest turned violent on November 26, 2022, after demonstrators prevented the Adani Group from resuming construction at the project site, where work had been suspended for four months. The construction at the port site subsequently resumed on the directions of the Kerala High Court.

item.description: The India Fix: A newsletter on Indian politics from Scroll.

Welcome to The India Fix by Shoaib Daniyal. A newsletter on Indian politics.

As always, if you’ve been sent this newsletter and like it, to get it in your inbox every week, sign up here (click on “follow”).

Las week, Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced in Parliament that India’s gross domestic product would hit the $5 trillion mark in 2029.

It’s a banal projection predicated on the simple maths of compounding. The Indian economy, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is growing so it will inevitably touch that mark one day. Yet, most Indians will be hit by an uncomfortable sense of deja vu when they read the phrase “$5 trillion economy”. It has functioned as a leitmotif of the Modi era, meant mostly to gaslight Indians about the true state of the economy.

item.title: From the biography: How mathematician DD Kosambi envisioned higher education in science in India
item.description: An excerpt form ‘DD Kosambi: One Life, Many Worlds’, by Ram Ramaswamy.
item.content:encoded:
When DD Kosambi was appointed Professor of Mathematics at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in June 1945, he was 38 years old. item.title: What decolonising economics can look like
item.description: The discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power have shaped economic development.
item.content:encoded:
Economics shapes many aspects of our daily lives, from the prices we pay to the policies governments adopt. Yet many of the ideas taught as universal principles of economics emerged from a narrow historical context and have rarely been examined through a decolonial lens.

A recently published book, Decolonizing Economics, argues that economics is long overdue for decolonisation. Its authors contend that the discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power shaped the development of modern economies and the economic theories used to explain them.

Decolonising economics means rethinking how we understand economic development and inequality. Rather than explaining prosperity through technology, markets and scientific progress, it examines how colonisation, resource extraction and exploited labour shaped today’s wealthy economies while contributing to underdevelopment elsewhere.

At its core, it’s about shifting away from an economy that benefits the elite to one that builds people’s capabilities.

As an economics professor, I’ve been restructuring my teaching based on my scholarship on critical microeconomics, critical macroeconomics and alternative ways to build the economy.

Questioning Eurocentric assumptions

The explosion took place in the head-race tunnel of the 500-MW Teesta VI hydropower project being constructed by NHPC, a public enterprise. Such tunnels are the main channels that route water from a river, and lead it to turbines to generate power, before channeling the water back to the river.

The explosion occurred after a “sudden burst of suspected methane gas trapped inside the rocks which led to an explosion generating dense fumes and toxic gases”, the company said in a press release.

While some workers on site escaped the explosion, 25 others were trapped after it triggered a rockfall and blocked the tunnel’s opening. Rescue operations began immediately and concluded on the third day. There were no survivors.

The company’s press release stated that it was carrying out a “detailed investigation” to “ascertain the cause of the incident”.

item.title: Roads in India are a deadly risk to the world’s smallest wild cat

item.content:encoded:
Scientists at the Wildlife Institute of India have reported two roadkill incidents of the rusty-spotted cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus) at the National Chambal Sanctuary in Etawah, Uttar Pradesh. The two records are the first documented occurrence of the small carnivore in southern Uttar Pradesh, according to the research paper published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa in May.

Roadkill data for small carnivores is heavily underreported, and these records were “a matter of chance”, according to Vishnupriya Kolipakam, a Wildlife Institute of India scientist and one of the paper’s authors.

While they add a new locality to the small cat’s known range, the wildlife sanctuary falls within its distribution range, Kolipakam said. “The wild cat has been reported from areas all around Chambal, including Kuno, Rangarh-Vishdhar, Ranthambhore, and Dholpur,” she said.

However, this follows a pattern, as seen in recent papers that have curated sighting reports of the strictly nocturnal cat. There were nine records of roadkill from the Saurashtra Peninsula in Gujarat between 2016 and 2024, and four records from Rajasthan between 2000 and 2020. In Nepal, too, where the cat was discovered as recently as 2016, there has been a record of a roadkill.

For an elusive small cat that has been rarely observed in the wild, these roadkill records add up to a significant number....

item.title: Using history and the present, a new book argues that Enlightenment ideals are not universal
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Chromatic World Order: The Fiction That Rules Our World: A Brief History of its Genesis and Other Stories’, by Sajid Mohamed.

When one considers the contradictions between the Enlightenment’s stated ideals and their practical implementation, for example, if we take the case of the American Revolution, which was one of the earliest implementations of the movement inspired by Enlightenment principles such as liberty, equality, and natural rights, and note that it coexisted with chattel slavery, we find that the Enlightenment ideals functioned as an ideological framework that could also coexist with, without any disturbance in its coexistence with a profoundly unequal and racialised society. Enslaved individuals could be, without needing an extraordinary example or explanation, constitutionally counted as three-fifths of a person for purposes of representation.

The US Constitution is an early, large-scale application of Enlightenment ideals that, at the same time, reveals the racially restricted claim to universality. Solomon Northup’s Twelve Years a Slave is a well-noted critique of the inconsistency of American democracy, particularly the coexistence of constitutional freedom and institutionalised slavery.

Northup, born a free Black man, who was enslaved and then later freed through legal intervention, appealed to reason and human dignity, and challenged, early on, the point being made here – that in the superficial universality of Enlightenment ideals within a racial order, Black or, by extension, coloured lives were expendable....

item.title: The ‘left-behind’ India: Global trade deals can have disruptive political consequences
item.description: The economic benefits are concentrated in a few places, deepening regional inequality and prompting migration which fuels nativist backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Amid talk of fractures in world trade, India continues to pursue globalisation as an economic development strategy. After a decade without any trade deals, India signed agreements with the European Union, United Kingdom, and New Zealand over 2025 and 2026, and is continuing negotiations with the US and other regions, signaling a renewed commitment to global economic integration. Most analyses of these agreements emphasise their geopolitical implications, especially for India’s emerging-power status and strategic relationship with the US, China, and Russia.

But these new deals will also contribute to the transformation of India’s domestic political economy. From India’s initial liberalisation in 1991, to its (re)emergence as a major exporter of textiles and apparel, to its dominant position in information technology services, globalisation has reshaped economic opportunity, social conflict, and political outcomes.

These new agreements, which grant extensive access to lucrative export markets, will likely catalyse deeper connections between India and the global economy.

item.title: Nairobi is bulldozing the Kibera settlement for a housing project, but who really benefits?
item.description: Kenya’s plan for affordable homes aims to redevelop one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.
item.content:encoded:
Bulldozers and construction crews are reshaping parts of Nairobi’s best-known informal settlement, Kibera. In a video shared by President William Ruto, new apartment blocks rise alongside existing corrugated-iron structures, while new roads cut through the settlement. The message is clear: Kenya’s affordable housing programme is bringing modern housing to one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.

The redevelopment forms part of Ruto’s broader affordable housing programme, which aims to deliver 200,000 housing units annually, combining social housing, affordable homes and market-rate units. By March 2026, government figures indicated that 8,367 units had been completed since Ruto took office in September 2022, with many more at various stages of construction across the country. Completed units therefore remain well below the programme’s stated annual target.

Supporters see it as a long-overdue investment in urban infrastructure and housing. Critics, however, have challenged the compulsory levy used to finance the programme: employees pay 1.5% of their gross monthly salary, matched by a 1.5% employer contribution, while people outside formal employment pay 1.5% of their gross income. They have also raised concerns about whether the homes will be affordable to lower-income households and allocated transparently.

item.title: ‘A lifetime of looking’: Arundhathi Subramanian on how Gieve Patel translated two Gujarati mystics

It feels only right to begin with an admission: I don’t think I understood what Gieve Patel’s translations meant to him until he died.

And yet, he offered clues. He once said that his translations had come into his life as a replacement for his own poetry. On another occasion, he said that he would sometimes spend an entire day looking at a translation in much the way he contemplated a painting in his studio. At the end of it, he would often do no more than delete a comma. He frequently said that the work was almost done, that he was “months away from closure”. But then, he seemed to have been saying that for almost as long as I have known him.

I will admit I had my own theories about Gieve’s reluctance to publish his translations. I attributed it to a hyper-self-critical strain, a perfectionist’s pride. Or writer’s block. I thought he was overthinking things. At times, I wondered if he felt he had lost his earlier sure-footedness. Perhaps he was simply preoccupied with his painting? item.title: Should India apologise for caste injustice, like Nepal did?
item.description: A formal apology may not lead to concrete changes. Instead, pursuing reparations could help reimagine the project of social justice in India.
item.content:encoded:
“Why should I have to pay for something my ancestors did?” That is a refrain frequently heard from members of the upper castes during discussions about casteist violence and prejudice or reservations in India.

This belief has found renewed expression in the “Reservation Hatao Movement”, a social media campaign that gained visibility in late July. It calls for the abolition of caste-based reservation so that “merit” and equal competition can prevail.

Many Indians believe that caste is a relic of a bygone time and that the government’s social justice policies have addressed these problems.

This ignores the inherited control over land, wealth, education, social networks and institutions through which caste privilege reproduces itself, presenting outcomes produced by historical inequality as though they emerged from neutral competition among equals.

The Indian state, similarly, speaks the language of social justice without unsettling the structures of social power that shape Indian society.

It is against the backdrop of this refusal of historical accountability that Nepal’s decision to offer a formal state apology to Dalits for centuries of caste-based oppression acquired significance in India. In April, referring to Nepal’s decision, MP Chandrashekhar Azad asked in Parliament when India would apologise to Dalits for centuries of injustice.

The Jharkhand government on Sunday agreed to cancel three examinations, including the preliminary examination of the 14th state Public Service Commission Combined Civil Services, after talks with two delegations of protesting student groups in Ranchi, The Indian Express reported.

The government also agreed to involve the Enforcement Directorate in an inquiry into alleged financial irregularities linked to the 14th Jharkhand Public Service Commission examination.

The decisions came as the students’ protest in Ranchi entered its 16th day. The protests began on July 25, inspired by the agitation across the country against the alleged mismanagement of national competitive exams. The protesters have been holding a sit-in at Ranchi’s Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium, with six demonstrators on a fast.

On Sunday, after the talks, the government announced that it would cancel the Jharkhand Public Service Commission backlog 2023 examination, the backlog 2025 examination and the preliminary examination. Three members of the commission also resigned on Sunday.

A backlog examination is a retest for candidates who failed a subject or missed the exam on their first attempt.

item.title: How to make the most of boredom
item.description: Boredom may be good for us if we effectively tap into its full potential.
item.content:encoded:
Boredom is something many of us will do everything we can to avoid. We fill our time with social media, books and TV programmes and keeping our schedules packed with plans.

But boredom doesn’t always need to be seen as something negative. Boredom may, in fact, be good for you – but only if you effectively tap into its full potential.

1. It can push you towards positive change

Boredom tends to arise when we want to be mentally engaged but our current activity or environment isn’t providing the level of challenge, stimulation or meaning we need. This can leave us feeling restless – especially if we don’t know how to remedy the situation.

It’s for this reason that boredom can be used to push ourselves towards change and encourage exploration.

But in order to make boredom really work for you, it’s vital to avoid just reaching for the next easy distraction, like scrolling on your phone, online shopping or visiting the pantry for a snack.

Positive change comes not from asking “how do I stop feeling like this?” but asking yourself “what meaningful thing do I need next?” Focusing on doing something meaningful is key to making boredom a bridge to more productive or positive activities.

It ended on a cogitative note when a guest innocently wondered what the animals in this dense, isolated ecosystem would say about the Great Nicobar project if they could talk.

I would like to think Tansy Troy somehow overheard this conversation.

The Great Nicobar Journey, an eco-adventure novel written by educationalist, activist, and poet Tansy Troy, looks at the Great Nicobar project from the point of view of the thousands of animals and birds on the island. item.title: On India’s western coastline, ‘ghost’ fishing gear is causing marine pollution
item.description: Damaged nets and their pieces slip into the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life.
item.content:encoded:
In the early light at Thoppumpady fishing harbour in the city of Kochi, coils of blue and green nylon nets lay heaped on the concrete docks, stiff with salt after a long night at sea. Many had been patched and repatched so often that they were barely holding together. Nets too damaged to mend are often cut loose offshore. Once they sink, few are ever recovered.

Across India’s west coast, lost fishing gear known as “ghost gear” has become a significant source of marine pollution. Nets vanish whole or in fragments, slipping into the waters of the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life long after fishers abandon them.

India operates one of the world’s largest marine fishing sectors, supporting an estimated 14.5 million livelihoods along more than 7,500 kilometres of coastline.

While national estimates are scarce, a 2022 study in the southwestern state of Kerala, where Kochi is located, found that fishers lost, abandoned or discarded about 21% of their fishing gear annually. That’s more than 10 times the global average of 1.82% estimated by another study, which highlights the scale of material entering India’s marine environment.

item.title: UPI to remain free for users, some merchants may face ‘nominal’ charges, says Centre
item.description: The clarification came after the Lok Sabha passed a bill allowing banks and other service providers to levy charges on UPI payments.
item.content:encoded:
Consumers making UPI payments will not face any transaction charges, said the Union government on Saturday.

“All person-to-person transactions will continue to be free of charge,” stated the Union Ministry of Finance.

The clarification came two days after the Lok Sabha passed the Taxation and Other Laws Amendment Bill 2026, which would allow banks and other service providers to levy charges on payments through UPI and RuPay debit cards.

The new bill would amend the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 and has led to fears that merchants, who would face a Merchant Discount Rate, would pass off the cost to consumers in the future.

Merchant Discount Rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

The United Payment Interface, or UPI, is a real-time payment system. In July, users made 2,366 crore UPI transactions worth Rs 29.9 lakh crore.

On Wednesday, the finance ministry stated that only a limited set of merchant transactions will attract the Merchant Discount Rate. The charges will apply “above a certain threshold and at a nominal rate”, it added.

item.title: ‘The belief that written language is more important than spoken is harming the Konkani movement’
item.description: An interview with Konkani-to-English literary translator Augusto Pinto.
item.content:encoded:
Sharing its name with the coast of its origin, the language of Konkani is spoken in multiple dialects and written in scripts as diverse as Perso-Arabic, Roman, Devanagari, Kannada, and Malayalam. Enmeshed within the politics of language, so closely tied to regional identity in South Asia, official status, standardisation, and patronage pertaining to the scripts and languages in which Goan literary production occurs have been matters of long-standing concern in the enclave.

Located on the Konkan coast, Goa’s linguistic and literary heritage outsizes the region’s diminutive geography. Konkani is one of the languages in which Goan writers have expressed their craft in Romi and Nagri scripts, but Goan literature also appears in Marathi, English, and Portuguese. In fact, among the first novels of South Asian nascence is Os Brahmanes (1866) by Goan writer Francisco Luís Gomes (1829-1869); its Portuguese title really requires no translation, although The Brahmans (1971) – an edition in English – does exist.

Despite this varied literary heritage, in addition to the controversies surrounding it, intra- and inter-language translation in Goa has been limited. While translation efforts alone cannot diminish internecine linguistic tensions, they may support dialogue across the borders between scripts and languages. item.title: In photos: How festivals and rituals help Koraput’s Adivasis keep local seed varieties alive
item.description: On World Indigenous Peoples Day, a glimpse at how agricultural biodiversity is woven into everyday life, preserving local knowledge over generations.
item.content:encoded:
The first pot of rice newly harvested during October-November is never eaten straight away in Koraput. Before families gather around the meal, a portion is offered to the village deity. Around five to six months later, the next farming season begins with prayers for rain, while wooden ploughs, cattle and seeds are honoured in their own ceremonies.

In Koraput, in the Eastern Ghats of southern Odisha, every stage of cultivation has its own festival. The region is home to the Paroja, Gadaba, Kondh, Bhumia, Bhottada, Durua and Saura Adivasi communities. Here, agriculture is intrinsically linked with culinary heritage and faith.

Koraput is among India’s richest centres of crop diversity. It harbours hundreds of locally adapted crop varieties, including indigenous paddy, finger millet, little millet, pigeon pea, black gram, horse gram, niger, sesame, traditional vegetables, tubers and wild edible plants.

Unlike monoculture farming, fields here are planted with a diverse mix of crops that support one another, reduce farming risks and provide food throughout the year. Farmers cultivate varieties of rice that mature at different times, ensuring that all crops do not ripen at once. This helps spread the risk when rainfall is delayed or uneven.
